John Doe, DOB: 09-02-1941, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today by video link with the ward team. He is a bedbound older adult residing in a nursing facility, and most of the history was provided by his named nurse and the weekday caregiver, who also maintain a seizure observation log.

The caregiving staff report variability in recent events, noting “one or three seizures last month” depending on which entries were counted as full events versus brief episodes without clear impairment. They describe brief behavioural arrest with unresponsiveness, occasional right arm tremor, and post-event confusion lasting up to 20 minutes. There has been no reported tongue biting or head injury. No clear daytime pattern; some episodes occurred around early morning care. The team deny intercurrent infection, but he has had reduced oral intake on some days.

He is currently on Levetiracetam 750 mg b.d. and Lamotrigine 50 mg b.d., administered crushed with soft food. He has tolerated these without rash or clear mood change. The nurse notes intermittent daytime somnolence and mild dizziness on sitting up, which may be multifactorial given his frailty and concurrent medications for blood pressure and constipation. They also report occasional myoclonic jerks during repositioning, which are not clearly time-linked to the recorded seizures.

Examination today was limited by the remote setting. He was rousable to voice, oriented to person, followed one-step commands inconsistently, with no focal asymmetry appreciated on gross limb movements. No cardiorespiratory distress. Skin intact with pressure-relief measures in place. Most observations were relayed by staff.

Plan:
- Continue current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for now given the nursing team’s report of “one or three seizures last month” and the uncertainty about which events represent definite seizures.
- The facility will maintain a structured seizure diary capturing: exact time, witnessed features (including eye deviation, limb involvement, automatisms), duration, recovery phase, possible triggers (missed doses, sleep disruption, infection), and pre-event observations.
- Arrange serum levels for Lamotrigine and routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC) through the nursing facility within the next two weeks to check for metabolic contributors and adherence proxies; ensure results are forwarded to the clinic.
- Request an in-reach community EEG if feasible to help characterise events, acknowledging the limitations in a bedbound patient.
- Nursing advice: maintain strict medication administration times, ensure hydration, and continue pressure-area care. Observe for any new focal deficits or prolonged events (>5 minutes), for which emergency protocols should be followed.
- We will review in 8–10 weeks via telemedicine with the same caregivers present and the updated seizure diary to guide any medication adjustments.

Please let me know if there are changes in his baseline cognition, suspected infection, or if the events escalate in frequency or duration before the planned review.

Yours sincerely

12 Bracken Close, Sydenham, London SE26 4HP

Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw today with his partner. He reports a remote history of mild traumatic brain injury in his early twenties without documented loss of consciousness beyond a brief daze, and no neurosurgical intervention. There is no known family history of seizure disorders. He does not drink alcohol to excess and denies recreational drug use. Sleep has been fragmented recently due to early work starts.

He describes daily events despite treatment trials in primary care. The typical episodes are reported as brief loss of awareness with stiffening and subsequent generalised shaking, sometimes preceded by a rising internal sensation and a metallic taste. His partner has witnessed several events and timed them at around 60–90 seconds, followed by tiredness and headache for up to an hour. He keeps a diary and notes TC one/d over the past month, with only two seizure-free days in that period. He has had two minor tongue bites but no significant injuries. There is no consistent morning predominance; they occur at variable times, including at work and at home. There is no clear catamenial pattern (not applicable), and no definite photic provocation.

Current medications: levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily, lamotrigine titrating currently at 50 mg twice daily; sertraline 50 mg once daily for mood. No known drug allergies. He has previously tried sodium valproate briefly but discontinued after weight gain and tremor. He reports good adherence, and his partner corroborates this. No recent intercurrent illness. He is not driving.

On examination today, he was alert and orientated with normal language and cranial nerve function. Motor, coordination, and gait were within normal limits. No focal neurological deficits were identified. Vital signs were stable.

Investigations to date: basic bloods last month (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, HbA1c, B12, folate, TSH) were within reference ranges. An MRI brain from 2019 (non-epilepsy protocol) was reported as normal. He has not had prolonged EEG monitoring; a routine EEG five years ago was normal.

Given the ongoing daily events (TC one/d) and the remote head injury, I discussed the value of updated epilepsy-protocol MRI and prolonged video-EEG monitoring to characterise the events and correlate semiology with electrographic findings. He is agreeable to proceeding. We also discussed general measures including regular sleep, hydration, and stress management as supportive strategies, and the importance of medication adherence, which he and his partner already prioritise.

Plan:
- Arrange video-EEG monitoring (inpatient if feasible) to capture typical events.
- Request epilepsy-protocol MRI brain.
- Continue current medication regimen pending further data; liaise with pharmacy to ensure uninterrupted supply.
- Seizure diary to be maintained, including possible triggers and timing.
- Provide workplace letter regarding safety considerations; he is currently not driving and understands DVLA requirements following seizures.
- Review in clinic after investigations or sooner if there is any escalation (prolonged events >5 minutes, clusters without recovery, or injury).

Many thanks for your referral. I will update you following the investigations.

Yours sincerely

I reviewed Bill in clinic today, accompanied by his key worker who has supported him for the last year. He reports increasing sensory intolerance to brightly lit, acoustically harsh environments. Over the last six months he describes more rapid-onset events with left facial pulling followed by jerking of the left arm, preserved awareness, then brief speech arrest. These episodes now arise chiefly during shifts near stage lighting rigs at his day centre and on the factory floor during machinery testing, with faster evolution than previously described.

Seizures: He remains abstinent from alcohol; however, he and staff note a pattern of attacks clustering after evenings spent in loud, high-glare venues at the centre, consistent with episodes that tend to follow exposure rather than intake. Frequency has increased: July x 3 focal aware motor; August x 4 focal aware motor (two progressing to impaired awareness); September x 5 focal aware motor with two focal to bilateral tonic–clonic. This represents a clear deterioration compared with earlier months when events were sporadic and slower in onset. A seizure diary kept by staff corroborates this trend, particularly on days involving rigging under bright LED arrays and during compressor testing.

Neurological examination: Alert and oriented; speech mildly hesitant. Subtle left nasolabial flattening at rest. Increased tone right lower limb with circumduction on gait testing; Romberg negative. No new cranial nerve deficits. Fundoscopy unremarkable. Cognitive screen shows slowed processing speed compared with prior review.

Epilepsy classification: The clinical semiology, consistent lateralising signs, and evolution support a diagnosis of focal epilepsy. There is no evidence of a primary generalised epilepsy syndrome.

Risk/precipitating factors: Photopic glare and complex acoustic environments appear to act as triggers. Sleep is fragmented on nights after late activities at the centre. No current alcohol use.

Plan:
- Acknowledge deterioration with increased event rate and faster evolution in bright, high-noise settings.
- Arrange urgent EEG with photic stimulation and patterned stimulus, plus prolonged ambulatory recording across a typical day at the centre if feasible.
- MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) to reassess focal cortical injury sequelae post-TBI.
- No immediate change to antiepileptic regimen today pending investigations; consider levetiracetam uptitration versus switch to lacosamide at next review, guided by EEG and tolerability.
- Provide written guidance to day centre to minimise triggers: reduce exposure to intense LED arrays, allow shaded rest areas, use hearing protection during machinery testing, scheduled breaks to reduce sensory load.
- Reinforce seizure diary with precise logging of lighting/sound exposure and sleep the preceding night.
- Check trough carbamazepine level, U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D.
- Bone health: continue Calcium/Vitamin D; DEXA due next year.

Follow-up: Review in 8 weeks, sooner if further focal to bilateral tonic–clonic events occur.

Yours sincerely,

Thank you for referring this patient for neurological review. I met him today in clinic accompanied by his partner. He described longstanding episodes that he and his family have termed “spells,” beginning in his late teens. The events are stereotyped: he experiences a brief warning of a rising internal tension and a sense of detachment, followed by behavioural arrest with fixed gaze and lip chewing reported by witnesses. On some occasions there is right arm stiffening and a brief cry. He is typically confused for 15–30 minutes afterwards and complains of a throbbing headache with pronounced fatigue.

Regarding periodicity, he and his partner report that the events tend to group together over several days in a repeating pattern roughly every four to five weeks. Within these burst periods the number of episodes varies and has not been reliably logged; outside these periods he may go a week or two without events. This “regular bursts every few weeks; number during bursts not well documented” pattern has been their usual experience for years. He started levetiracetam six months ago after trials of lamotrigine and carbamazepine were discontinued for rash and dizziness respectively. Notably, since commencing current therapy the overall pattern has persisted without clear change in frequency or recovery time.

There is no consistent relationship with sleep deprivation or alcohol, though he suspects that high work stress and missed meals may act as triggers. No tongue laceration or incontinence has been witnessed. He has had two emergency attendances in the last year for cluster days with prolonged confusion; bloods at those times were unremarkable and a CT head performed three years ago was reported normal. He has never had status epilepticus or significant injury from these events. Family history is non-contributory. He does not drive and is aware of DVLA guidance as previously discussed with his GP.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal speech, cranial nerves intact, no focal motor deficit, and normal coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. There were no features of ongoing post-event confusion at the time of review. Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular.

We discussed next steps. The main issue at present is to clarify the nature of the events and obtain objective correlation. He is agreeable to an ambulatory EEG with event diary, followed by consideration of inpatient video-EEG if the ambulatory study does not capture typical episodes. I have also recommended structured documentation using a calendar or smartphone app to record the timing of warning symptoms, event duration, and recovery features, so that we can quantify numbers during the clustered periods. He will continue levetiracetam at his current dose as he reports tolerability but no perceived benefit so far; we will not change treatment until we have more diagnostic information. I have requested routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D) to be done at his GP surgery for baseline monitoring.

For safety, we reinforced standard advice around adequate sleep, regular meals, moderated alcohol intake, and seeking urgent help if any event lasts more than five minutes, occurs back-to-back without recovery, or if he sustains significant injury. He understands not to swim unsupervised, to avoid heights, and to take showers instead of baths.

I will review him in clinic after the ambulatory EEG. Thank you again for the referral and for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there is any additional history or prior imaging that would be helpful to obtain before telemetry.

Yours sincerely

Thank you for referring your patient, whom I reviewed in our neurology clinic today. He attended with his paper seizure calendar, which he has kept meticulously for the past year and brings to each appointment. This allowed a structured discussion of recent events. 

From his calendar and his account, he experiences brief focal aware episodes characterised by a rising epigastric sensation, facial pallor, and a momentary speech arrest; on occasion these evolve into focal impaired awareness seizures with right-hand automatisms and subsequent confusion lasting 10–15 minutes. In addition, he reports intermittent generalised tonic–clonic seizures, typically without warning and followed by myalgia and headache for several hours. The calendar indicates a pattern of seizures recurring in short bursts around the beginning of most months shortly after waking, with quieter intervals between these bursts. He records that the focal aware events often precede the larger events by 24–48 hours. 

In terms of frequency, his paper log demonstrates repeated short runs around month‑end to mid‑month, mainly noted on waking in the early morning, with two months showing additional daytime events under stress. This pattern has been consistent since spring this year. He has not used a smartphone app and prefers his dated paper grid, which includes tick boxes for type and timing; he brought copies of the last three months for scanning into the record. 

On current assessment, the epilepsy is best classified as Combined Generalised and Focal Epilepsy. He has both generalised seizures (convulsions without clear warning) and focal seizures (epigastric aura with automatisms and impaired awareness), as corroborated by the semiology he described and the timing patterns in his calendar. There is no current history suggestive of absence seizures or myoclonic jerks, and there is no clear photic trigger. He denies nocturnal tongue biting or enuresis outside of the recorded convulsions. 

He reports good adherence to medication, with occasional missed evening doses during periods of shift work; he has started using a pillbox aligned to the calendar dates to mitigate this. He does not drive. Sleep deprivation and missed meals appear to precede the early‑morning events. Alcohol intake is modest and there is no recreational drug use. No recent head injury. Family history is negative for epilepsy. 

Examination today was unremarkable with normal cranial nerves, tone, power, coordination and gait; no lateralising signs were elicited. Interim bloods from the GP (FBC, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, vitamin D) were within reference limits last month. 

Plan: I have requested an updated EEG with sleep deprivation and extended montage to better capture interictal features, as well as a brain MRI with epilepsy protocol for structural correlation. I have asked him to continue bringing his paper seizure calendar to all appointments and to annotate each event with time of day, type, and any missed doses or sleep loss, as this has been extremely helpful in clarifying the pattern. We will review in clinic after the investigations to consider optimisation of therapy in light of the combined generalised and focal features. He understands the DVLA guidance relevant to his current situation and agrees to maintain seizure precautions at home. 

Yours sincerely
